items.prompt: Per L1, what is "onboarding"?
choices: A deliberate design problem — getting someone new productive in a role, not just handing over information and waiting
The specific paperwork and compliance forms a new hire fills out on their very first day
A single meeting where a manager briefly introduces a new hire to the rest of the team
Whatever documentation a company happens to already have written down somewhere
items.explanation: L1 frames onboarding as a deliberate design problem — something to be planned, not just information handed over passively.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, was the new hire's onboarding plan careless or lazy?
choices: No — the Scenario states nothing about the plan was lazy or careless, yet the new hire still ended up far behind
Yes — the manager quite clearly didn't put any real thought into the plan at all
Yes, but only because the internal wiki itself happened to be poorly written
The Scenario deliberately doesn't say one way or another whether the plan was careless
items.explanation: L1's closing question is explicit that nothing about the plan was lazy or careless — the failure came from the plan's structure, not from a lack of effort.

items.prompt: What is a "ramp plan"?
choices: A structured sequence of increasingly larger tasks that builds a new hire's context and confidence gradually, rather than requiring full context up front
A single, large document meant to cover every system a new hire might eventually touch
A completely fixed script that never changes at all once a new hire starts
A formal test given to new hires specifically to see how much they already know
items.explanation: A ramp plan is specifically about gradual, sequenced task-building — not a document, a test, or a fixed unchanging script.

items.prompt: Per L1, how does a ramp plan solve both "too little structure" and "too much at once" simultaneously?
choices: By giving a small, real, scoped first task early, with the rest of the context introduced only when it's actually needed for the next task
By giving a new hire the exact same 40-page wiki, just spread out gradually over more weeks
By removing all structure entirely so the new hire can decide everything on their own
By requiring a new hire to pass a formal written exam before starting any real work at all
items.explanation: L1 describes the ramp plan's mechanism directly: a small scoped task early, with further context introduced just-in-time rather than all at once or not at all.

items.prompt: What is an "onboarding buddy"?
choices: A specific teammate, not the manager, a new hire can ask small, frequent questions of without scheduling a meeting
The new hire's own direct manager, who also handles every scheduled check-in
A software tool specifically built to answer onboarding questions automatically
A mentor who's assigned only for the new hire's very first performance review
items.explanation: L1 defines the buddy specifically as a low-overhead teammate contact distinct from the manager, not a tool or a review-cycle role.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does a ramp plan typically include a buddy in addition to a manager check-in?
choices: Small, frequent questions need a low-overhead answer path that a scheduled, infrequent manager check-in can't provide
The buddy is meant to fully replace the need for any manager involvement at all
Buddies are described as only being needed for new hires who happen to work remotely
There's no real reason for this — it's just a common tradition with no functional purpose at all
items.explanation: L1 ties the buddy directly to the mismatch between how often small questions come up and how infrequent scheduled manager check-ins are.

items.prompt: What does "time-to-first-contribution" measure?
choices: How long it takes a new hire to ship something real and working, however small
How many total pages of documentation a new hire has already read
How many separate meetings a new hire has attended during their first week
How long a new hire's very first formal performance review actually takes
items.explanation: Time-to-first-contribution is specifically about shipping something real, not about reading volume or meeting attendance.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, by week 2 what had the new hire actually shipped?
choices: Nothing — the check-in found they hadn't shipped a single change
One small, carefully scoped bug fix, shipped early and cleanly
A full, complete feature, though it shipped with several lingering bugs
The Scenario deliberately doesn't mention whether anything was shipped by then
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that by the week-2 check-in the new hire hadn't shipped anything at all — a concrete sign the plan wasn't working.

items.prompt: Per L1, what does the new hire's situation in the Scenario suggest about doing everything they were asked?
choices: Doing everything asked isn't enough on its own if the plan itself wasn't structured to build usable context
It proves the new hire simply wasn't reading the material carefully enough
It proves that 40 pages is always too much to read, regardless of how it's structured
It shows that reading documentation is never genuinely useful during onboarding at all
items.explanation: L1's closing question makes exactly this point — following the plan exactly still left the new hire behind, which points at the plan's design, not the new hire's effort.

items.prompt: By week 3 in the Scenario, what specific gap remained even after reading the full wiki?
choices: The new hire still didn't know who to ask about which system
The new hire had completely forgotten how to use their own development tools
The new hire had already quietly left the company by that point
The new hire had already been assigned a buddy but had never once used them
items.explanation: The Scenario specifically states that by week 3 the new hire still didn't know who owned which part of the system — a gap the wiki alone didn't close.

items.prompt: What is "cognitive overload" in this unit's framework?
choices: The failure mode where too much unanchored information is presented at once, so little of it is retained because none of it connects yet to something the person is actually doing
A specific medical condition that's entirely unrelated to onboarding design
The state of simply having too many meetings scheduled in a single day
Just a synonym for having too little documentation actually available
items.explanation: Cognitive overload is specifically about unanchored information failing to stick — not meeting volume or a lack of documentation.
items.reference:
Cognitive overload
🧠 Too much, unanchored, all at once
🔗 Nothing connects to a real task yet
Why: the Scenario's 40-page wiki is a textbook case.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does the Scenario's wiki dump produce cognitive overload even though the new hire read all of it?
choices: None of it was anchored to something the new hire was actually doing, so little of it stuck
The wiki itself happened to contain several factually incorrect statements
The new hire simply didn't spend enough total hours actually reading it
Cognitive overload is described as only happening when material is read too quickly
items.explanation: L1 ties cognitive overload to a lack of anchoring, not reading speed, effort, or accuracy of the material itself.
items.reference:
Cognitive overload
🧠 Too much, unanchored, all at once
🔗 Nothing connects to a real task yet
Why: the Scenario's 40-page wiki is a textbook case.

items.prompt: Per L1, is time-to-first-contribution the same thing as how much material has been "covered"?
choices: No — it's a separate, concrete signal about whether the ramp plan is actually working
Yes — the two terms are described as meaning exactly the same thing in this unit
Yes, because covering more material is described as always speeding up shipping
L1 deliberately doesn't distinguish between these two particular ideas at all
items.explanation: L1 explicitly separates time-to-first-contribution from material coverage — one measures real output, the other just measures reading volume.
items.reference:
Time-to-first-contribution
🚢 Shipped something real
📖 Not the same as pages read
Why: the Scenario's new hire covered 100% of the wiki and still shipped nothing.

items.prompt: Per L1, could a new hire have "covered" 100% of the assigned material and still have a poor time-to-first-contribution?
choices: Yes — the Scenario is exactly this case: everything was read, and nothing had shipped by week 2
No — covering all of the assigned material is described as guaranteeing a fast contribution
No, because coverage and time-to-first-contribution are explicitly defined as identical
This can only ever happen if the new hire is being deliberately slow on purpose
items.explanation: The Scenario is precisely this situation — full coverage of the wiki, but no shipped contribution, showing the two measures can diverge sharply.
items.reference:
Time-to-first-contribution
🚢 Shipped something real
📖 Not the same as pages read
Why: the Scenario's new hire covered 100% of the wiki and still shipped nothing.

items.prompt: Per L2, is "look around and ask questions" a lighter, gentler version of the Scenario's information dump?
choices: No — it's the same underlying mistake from the opposite direction, since it also leaves a new hire with no task to anchor exploration to
Yes — giving no structure at all is described as always strictly better than too much
Yes, because it requires noticeably less reading than working through a 40-page wiki
There's genuinely no real relationship at all between these two particular approaches
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames both approaches as the same root failure — unstructured information with nothing to anchor it to — from opposite directions.

items.prompt: Per L2, would simply giving the Scenario's new hire a shorter document have fixed the underlying problem?
choices: Not by itself — a shorter document with the same "read it, then we'll talk" structure still isn't anchored to anything the new hire is doing
Yes — any document that's under 10 pages is described as avoiding the failure entirely
Yes, because document length is described as the only variable that actually matters
No, because no amount of documentation is ever described as useful in onboarding at all
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that the problem isn't the wiki's length — it's that reading came before doing, which a shorter document alone doesn't fix.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what comes immediately after a new hire ships their first small task?
choices: Progressively larger tasks over weeks 2-4, with more autonomy and less hand-holding
A single, large document meant to cover the rest of the entire system
A formal written exam covering absolutely everything discussed so far
The entire onboarding process is considered fully complete at that point
items.explanation: L2's flowchart sequences weeks 2-4 as progressively larger tasks with increasing autonomy — not a document dump or a final exam.

items.prompt: Per L2, what is a 30/60/90 checkpoint for?
choices: Comparing actual progress against what the ramp plan expected, and adjusting the plan if needed
Deciding specifically whether to extend a new hire's probationary period
A completely fixed script that must be followed exactly, regardless of how the new hire is actually doing
Measuring specifically how many pages of documentation the new hire has read so far
items.explanation: L2 frames the 30/60/90 checkpoint as a comparison-and-adjustment point, not a fixed script or a documentation-reading metric.

items.prompt: Per L2, why is a scheduled, infrequent manager check-in a poor fit for a new hire's early questions?
choices: It matches exactly the cadence that let the Scenario's two-week gap grow unnoticed, when small questions are actually most frequent
Managers are described as never being available to new hires under any circumstances
Manager check-ins are described as being unnecessary at any point during onboarding
There's genuinely no real downside here — a manager check-in works just as well as a buddy does
items.explanation: L2 ties the manager check-in's infrequency directly to the Scenario's own two-week gap — exactly the mismatch a buddy is meant to close.

items.prompt: Per L2, when is the volume of small "what does this mean" questions typically highest for a new hire?
choices: In the early days, which is exactly when a low-overhead buddy matters most
After the new hire has already been in the role for well over a year
Only during the new hire's very first scheduled meeting with the team
The volume of such small questions is described as constant and unchanging over time entirely
items.explanation: L2 explicitly ties the buddy's value to the early days, when this kind of small, frequent question is at its highest volume.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with treating more documentation as the fix for a bad onboarding experience?
choices: The Scenario's new hire read everything they were given — the volume wasn't the failure, the lack of a task to anchor it to was
More documentation is described as always being strictly better, with no real downside
Documentation is only ever considered a problem if it happens to be poorly formatted
This particular failure mode is described as not applying to the Scenario at all
items.explanation: L2's failure modes table makes exactly this point — the Scenario's new hire didn't fail to read; the plan failed to anchor what was read to a task.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, is leaving a new hire with no starting point the same as giving them real autonomy?
choices: No — it's the same lack of structure as an information dump, just from the other direction
Yes — any amount of structure at all is described as harmful to a new hire's autonomy
Yes, and it's described as always being strictly better than having a ramp plan
This particular comparison isn't addressed anywhere at all at this level
items.explanation: L2's failure modes table is explicit that "look around and ask questions" isn't a lighter version of a ramp plan — it's the same underlying lack of structure.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, what does Day 1 consist of?
choices: Environment set up, a small real scoped first task, and an assigned buddy — together, not a reading assignment
Reading through the entire internal wiki before touching anything else at all
A formal written exam covering the full codebase on day one itself
Nothing specific at all — Day 1 is left entirely unstructured in the diagram
items.explanation: L2's flowchart bundles environment setup, a scoped task, and a buddy into Day 1 — not a reading assignment.
items.reference:
The ramp-plan sequence
1️⃣ Day 1: setup + task + buddy
📈 Weeks 2-4: bigger tasks, less hand-holding
Why: doing starts immediately, not after reading.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, does the first real task wait until after the new hire has studied the system?
choices: No — the scoped first task is part of Day 1 itself, before broader study happens
Yes — the diagram shows a full week of reading before any real task even begins
Yes, but only specifically for new hires without any prior industry experience
The diagram deliberately doesn't specify exactly when the first task happens
items.explanation: L2's flowchart places the first real task on Day 1, not after a separate study period.
items.reference:
The ramp-plan sequence
1️⃣ Day 1: setup + task + buddy
📈 Weeks 2-4: bigger tasks, less hand-holding
Why: doing starts immediately, not after reading.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does context arriving "exactly when it's needed" work better than pre-loading it?
choices: It's immediately put to use instead of just being stored, unlike information given before there's a task to apply it to
It's simply a smaller total amount of information overall, nothing more
It completely removes the need for having a buddy at all during onboarding
It guarantees that the new hire will genuinely never need to ask a single question
items.explanation: L2 frames just-in-time context as valuable because it's used immediately, not because it's shorter or removes support structures.
items.reference:
Just-in-time context
⏱️ Arrives when a task needs it
✅ Used immediately, not stored
Why: unused information is what gets forgotten.

items.prompt: Per L2, what happens to context that's introduced with no immediate use for it?
choices: It tends to be forgotten by the time it's actually needed
It's always retained perfectly well by the new hire, regardless of timing
It actually becomes more valuable to the new hire the longer it sits unused
L2 deliberately doesn't address what happens to that kind of unused context
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that unanchored, unused context is exactly what tends to be forgotten before it's needed.
items.reference:
Just-in-time context
⏱️ Arrives when a task needs it
✅ Used immediately, not stored
Why: unused information is what gets forgotten.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, specifically why does "look around, ask questions" fail as an onboarding approach?
choices: With no scoped first task, there's no way to tell what matters yet — exploration has no direction
It fails specifically because it involves far too much reading overall
It fails only because it doesn't happen to involve an assigned buddy
L2's table deliberately doesn't include this particular approach at all
items.explanation: L2's table attributes this approach's failure to having no scoped starting point, not to reading volume or buddy absence.
items.reference:
The three approaches
📚 Dump: unanchored, all at once
🧭 Look around: no starting point at all
Why: both leave the new hire without a task to anchor to.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what do the information dump and the "look around" approach have in common?
choices: Both hand someone unstructured information (or an unstructured situation) and expect them to figure out on their own what matters right now
Both are described as requiring exactly the same total amount of reading
Both approaches were shown to work equally well in the Scenario, per L2's table
Neither approach is described as involving the new hire doing any real work at all
items.explanation: L2's table frames both approaches as unstructured — one with too much material, one with none — sharing the same root failure.
items.reference:
The three approaches
📚 Dump: unanchored, all at once
🧭 Look around: no starting point at all
Why: both leave the new hire without a task to anchor to.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the day-1 task need to be a small, real task rather than a toy exercise built specifically for onboarding?
choices: A toy exercise teaches the tools but not the system — a small real task teaches both the tools and how the actual codebase, review process, and team norms work
Toy exercises are described as being impossible to create for most engineering roles
Real tasks are described as always being faster to complete than toy exercises, regardless of scope
There's genuinely no real difference at all between these two particular approaches
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that a toy exercise teaches only the tools, while a real task simultaneously teaches the system, review process, and team norms.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the purpose of the environment-setup step on day 1, before the first real task?
choices: It confirms the tools work — via a trivial change like a typo fix — before anything harder depends on them working
It's meant to be the new hire's primary and only contribution for their entire first week
It's meant to fully replace the need for having a scoped first task at all
It's purely a formality on day one with no real practical purpose behind it
items.explanation: L3 frames the environment-setup step as a low-stakes confirmation that the tooling works, deliberately separate from the real first task that follows.

items.prompt: Per L3, once the day-1 task ships, what happens to the original 40-page wiki?
choices: It's still useful, but pieces of it become relevant exactly when a task the new hire is doing touches that part of the system, rather than being assigned all at once
It's discarded entirely at that point and never referenced again by anyone
It becomes the new hire's sole, mandatory reading assignment for the entirety of week 2
It's rewritten completely from scratch before the new hire can use any of it again
items.explanation: L3 explicitly keeps the wiki useful, but repositions it as just-in-time reference material tied to specific tasks, not a day-1 assignment.

items.prompt: Per L3, what happens to the buddy's level of involvement across weeks 2-4?
choices: It gradually decreases as the new hire needs less hand-holding
It actually increases steadily every single week, without exception
It stays exactly constant and unchanged from day 1 all the way through week 4
The buddy stops being involved in the process entirely right after day 1
items.explanation: L3 describes the buddy's involvement decreasing gradually as tasks grow and the new hire needs progressively less hand-holding.

items.prompt: Per L3, does a senior engineer joining from another company need the same ramp plan as a junior hire?
choices: The underlying mechanism still applies, but the structure should shift toward org-context rather than technical hand-holding, which the senior hire usually needs less of
No — seniority alone means no ramp plan or structure is ever needed at all
Yes, with absolutely no difference at all in what the structure should actually emphasize
Senior hires are described as never needing an assigned buddy under any circumstances
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the mechanism (small real task, just-in-time context) still holds, but what needs structuring shifts toward org-context for an experienced hire.

items.prompt: Per L3, what kind of context is a senior transplant more likely to be missing than a junior hire?
choices: Org-context — who makes which decisions, which parts of the system are considered fragile, and where team conventions diverge from general best practice
The basic technical skills needed to read and reason about unfamiliar code generally
Nothing at all — a senior hire is described as missing exactly the same things a junior hire would
How to use a basic text editor or a version control system like git
items.explanation: L3 specifically identifies org-context — decision-makers, fragile systems, local conventions — as what a senior transplant is usually missing, not baseline technical skill.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's wrong with assuming a senior hire needs no ramp plan at all?
choices: A senior transplant still needs structure — just retargeted toward org-context and history rather than technical hand-holding
Nothing at all is wrong with that assumption — seniority is described as making ramp plans entirely unnecessary
This particular issue is described as only applying to hires with less than five years of experience
Senior hires are described as onboarding themselves fully automatically, with no support needed at all
items.explanation: L3's failure modes table warns against skipping structure for senior hires entirely — the structure should be retargeted, not removed.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's the risk of treating a ramp plan as a fixed script that never changes?
choices: Without checking it against how the new hire is actually doing at each checkpoint, it can't catch and correct a real gap the way a 30/60/90 review would
There's genuinely no real risk here — a fixed script is described as always the safest possible choice
The only real risk at all is that it takes slightly longer to write out in full ahead of time
Fixed scripts are described as being impossible to create at all for any given role
items.explanation: L3's failure modes table warns specifically that a plan never compared against actual progress can't adjust to catch a real gap forming.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does week 1 include a pairing or review session built in?
choices: So the new hire sees how feedback and review norms actually work on this team, rather than reading about them
It's purely a social nicety with no real connection at all to the ramp plan's actual goals
It's meant to fully replace the need for having a day-1 task at all
It's only ever included for new hires who happen to specifically ask for it
items.explanation: L3 ties the week-1 pairing session directly to experiencing real review norms firsthand, not reading about them abstractly.
items.reference:
Week 1
🚢 Ship the day-1 task
👥 Pairing/review built in
Why: norms are experienced, not just described.

items.prompt: Per L3, is experiencing a real review firsthand different from reading about the team's review process?
choices: Yes — L3 specifically distinguishes seeing how feedback and review norms actually work from reading about them
No — L3 treats reading about the team's review norms as being equally effective
No, because week 1 is described as not actually involving any review activity at all
L3 deliberately doesn't address the team's review norms anywhere in its content
items.explanation: L3 explicitly favors direct experience of review norms over documentation about them, in week 1's design.

Week 1
🚢 Ship the day-1 task
👥 Pairing/review built in
Why: norms are experienced, not just described.

Yes — the core lesson is described as specific to engineering roles and doesn't transfer elsewhere
Yes, but only specifically for companies that are structured as remote-first
L3 deliberately doesn't address whether the core lesson generalizes beyond engineering

What generalizes

🔧 Task shape is what's specific here

choices: The exact shape of the tasks — environment setup, a scoped bug fix, a 30/60/90 checkpoint
The general idea that structure itself should expand gradually over time
The general idea that context should be anchored to something the person is currently doing

items.prompt: Per L3's extend-it question, what does it ask the reader to work out for a support or operations new hire instead of an engineer?
choices: What the equivalent of a small, real, scoped first task would look like, and whether the buddy's role would change
How to write an entirely new, full 40-page wiki tailored specifically to that role
Whether onboarding is even necessary at all for roles outside of engineering
How to entirely skip the day-1 environment-setup step for that kind of role
items.explanation: L3's extend-it question specifically asks the reader to re-derive what a scoped first task and buddy role look like outside engineering.

Extend it
🔀 Different role, same mechanism
❓ What's the equivalent first task?
Why: testing whether the mechanism transfers, not just the example.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does a support or operations role make "a small, real, scoped first task" harder to define than for an engineer?
choices: Because "shipping a small change" doesn't map onto a single well-defined task the same way a bug fix does
Because support and operations roles are described as never having any real tasks to assign
Because L3 explicitly claims onboarding doesn't apply at all to non-engineering roles
Because support roles are described as requiring absolutely no ramp plan at all
items.explanation: L3 notes the difficulty is that a support/ops role lacks an obvious single-task equivalent to a bug fix, not that onboarding doesn't apply.
